capstone: End-to-end DBA handover project: provision a containerized database server from scratch, configure memory and storage layout, harden it with least-privilege roles and auditing, implement automated backups with verified restores meeting a stated RPO/RTO, establish a monitoring baseline with working alerts, migrate a sample application database onto it with a documented cutover and rollback plan, and deliver a runbook an on-call successor could use at 3 AM. Present the runbook and a 10-minute walkthrough of one restore drill.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Explain in your own words why data files and log files should live on separate volumes.
What happens if the engine's max memory setting is left unbounded on a shared host, and how would you detect it?
Name three features gated to paid editions and describe how you would plan around each on a free edition.
Rebuild your container instance from scratch using only your setup notes. Did anything require guessing?
keyConcepts: Editions and licensing concepts: which features are gated behind paid editions
Physical file layout: data files, transaction logs, and temp/scratch space
Instance vs database vs schema terminology and how vendors differ
Memory architecture: buffer pool/cache and max server memory settings
Collation and character sets: chosen at install time, painful to change later
Service accounts and file-system permissions for database processes
Containerized deployment: volumes for persistence, ports, environment variables
Repeatable installs: documenting every choice so the build is reproducible
labs: Install SQL Server Developer Edition (or run the official container image) and document every setup choice in a lab journal.
Deploy Oracle Database Free in a container with persistent volume mounts; restart the container and prove data survives the restart.
Cap the engine's max memory at roughly half of host RAM, capture the before/after settings, and record the exact commands used.
Create a sample database with data and log files on separate paths; sketch the resulting file layout.
Stand up a second containerized instance with a different collation/character set and note what breaks when applications assume the default.
objectives: Install a free database engine (SQL Server Developer or Oracle Database Free) via installer or container with a repeatable, documented process.
Configure server-level memory limits and storage layout so the database does not starve its host.
Compare editions and licensing concepts at a planning level, including which features free editions lack.
Verify the install with a smoke test: create a database, create a table, and round-trip data through it.
modules.title: Installation and Configuration

checkpoints: A business states RPO 15 minutes and RTO 2 hours. Sketch the backup schedule and justify each piece.
One log backup in the middle of the chain is missing. Which restores are still possible, and which are lost?
Why is a backup file stored on the same disk as the database not a real backup?
Perform your restore drill from your notes alone and time it against the stated RTO.
keyConcepts: Full vs differential vs transaction-log/incremental backups and when each is used
Recovery models (simple vs full logging) and their trade-offs
RPO: how much data the business can afford to lose; RTO: how fast you must be back
Point-in-time recovery and why the log chain must stay unbroken
Backup verification: checksums, test restores, and treating untested backups as no backups
Off-host copies and the 3-2-1 rule concept for backup copies
Managed backup tooling concepts (e.g., RMAN catalogs) vs native backup commands
Corruption detection: page checksums and consistency checks
labs: Take a full backup of a lab database, then a differential and a log backup; record the size and duration of each.
Simulate a disaster: drop a table, then restore the database to the minute before the drop using the log chain.
Break the chain on purpose (change recovery model mid-sequence or skip a log backup) and document exactly how the restore fails.
Script an automated nightly backup with a verification step that restores to a staging database and reports success or failure.
Run a consistency check against a lab database and interpret the output line by line.
objectives: Distinguish full, differential, and log/incremental backups and explain when each is used.
Translate business RPO/RTO statements into a concrete backup schedule.
Perform complete point-in-time restores in a lab and verify data integrity afterward.
Adopt the discipline that an untested backup is not a backup: schedule and document restore drills.
modules.title: Backup and Recovery

checkpoints: Synchronous replication offers zero data loss but costs latency. Explain why in one paragraph.
Your standby is 45 minutes behind when the primary dies. What is the business impact in RPO/RTO terms?
Why must a failover be rehearsed before it is ever needed?
keyConcepts: High availability (uptime) vs disaster recovery (survivability): different problems, different tools
Synchronous vs asynchronous replication and the durability/latency trade-off
Failover vs switchover; automatic vs manual promotion
Quorum and witness concepts for preventing split-brain
Readable secondaries and offloading reporting workloads
Replication lag: how to measure it and when to alert on it
Failover drills: planned rehearsals vs real failures
The cost/complexity ladder: single instance, log shipping, replicas, clusters
labs: Build log-shipping-style replication between two free-edition instances using scheduled backup/restore jobs (the concept behind asynchronous DR).
Apply a write load to the primary and measure replication lag on the standby.
Simulate a primary failure: promote the standby manually and document every step and decision.
Research which HA features are unavailable in free editions and write a one-page brief on what would require a paid edition.
Design an HA/DR topology on paper for a fictional small business with RPO 1 hour and RTO 4 hours, and defend it in writing.
objectives: Compare failover clustering, synchronous replicas, and asynchronous replication in plain language.
Explain the difference between high availability and disaster recovery.
Describe Always On availability concepts and Data Guard concepts at the concept level.
Design an HA/DR topology for a given RPO/RTO on paper.
modules.title: High Availability and Replication

checkpoints: Why is a db_owner/DBA-level account for an application a finding, and what do you replace it with?
You restore an encrypted backup to a new server and it fails. What is missing, and why?
Which events belong in the audit trail for a database that holds personal data?
Explain the difference between encrypting the disk and encrypting the database itself.
keyConcepts: Least privilege and separation of duties in database access
Authentication modes: OS/integrated logins vs database-native logins
Server roles vs database roles vs custom application roles
Auditing: capturing logins, schema changes, and access to sensitive tables
Encryption at rest (transparent data encryption concepts) and key management basics
Encryption in transit (TLS) and certificate concepts
Surface-area reduction: disabling unused features and services
Patching cadence and vulnerability scanning as ongoing hygiene
labs: Create three personas (application service account, analyst, administrator) with tailored roles; prove the analyst cannot write and the app account cannot read outside its schema.
Enable auditing of logins and schema changes, perform suspicious actions, then find them in the audit trail.
Enable TLS for client connections on a containerized instance and verify the connection is actually encrypted.
Enable at-rest encryption on a lab database, then back it up and restore it elsewhere to observe the key/certificate dependency firsthand.
Run a hardening checklist against your lab instance, remediate every finding, and document each remediation.
objectives: Apply least privilege by creating logins and users with only the permissions their job requires.
Implement role-based access with custom database roles instead of built-in privileged roles.
Enable auditing of logins and sensitive actions and practice reading the audit trail.
Configure encryption at rest and in transit at the feature level on a lab instance.
modules.title: Security Hardening

checkpoints: Wait statistics shift overnight from CPU to I/O. What changed, and what do you check first?
Your space alert fires at 3 AM for transaction-log growth. What does the runbook say?
How do you tell blocking apart from a deadlock, and why does the distinction matter?
Define 'normal' for your lab server in three sentences using your own baseline.
keyConcepts: Wait statistics: learning what the server is actually waiting on
Blocking and deadlocks: detection, victim selection, and resolution concepts
Space monitoring: data files, log files, temp/scratch space, and OS disk
Slow-query capture: finding top queries by duration and logical reads
Baselines, trends, and seasonal patterns: defining abnormal before it happens
Alert design: thresholds tied to baselines, severity levels, and runbooks
Error logs and job history as the first place to look when something breaks
Dashboards vs alerts: observation vs notification are different jobs
labs: Capture a baseline of wait statistics, file sizes, and top queries over several runs and store it in a workbook.
Generate blocking on purpose with two concurrent sessions; identify the blocker and the victim using system views.
Create a deadlock in the lab, read the deadlock report, and explain the cycle in plain language.
Fill a scratch volume safely inside a container and watch space monitoring react; document the remediation steps.
Build a one-page dashboard (even a spreadsheet) from your baseline metrics.
objectives: Identify the five health signals that matter most: waits, locks, space, slow queries, and errors.
Build a performance baseline so that 'abnormal' has a concrete definition.
Configure alerts with thresholds tied to the baseline while avoiding alert fatigue.
Read an execution plan at a basic level and find the most expensive operator.
modules.title: Monitoring and Alerting

checkpoints: A query is slow for one customer but fast for everyone else. What is your first hypothesis?
You added an index and nothing improved. What do you check next?
When is 'add more hardware' the wrong answer to a slow query?
Explain the most expensive operator in a query plan to a non-DBA in plain language.
keyConcepts: The triage method: scope, measure, hypothesize, change one thing, verify
Reading execution plans: scans vs seeks, key lookups, sorts, and spills
Parameter sniffing concepts: why the same query performs differently with different inputs
Statistics: what the optimizer knows about your data and when it goes stale
Indexing fundamentals: clustered vs nonclustered structures and covering concepts
Temp/scratch space pressure and its symptoms
Knowing when the problem is not the database: app, network, or storage
Incident documentation: timeline, root cause, and prevention
labs: Load a sample dataset, run a deliberately slow query, capture its plan, and identify the most expensive operator.
Create the index the plan suggests and measure before/after performance with the same workload.
Simulate stale statistics in a lab-only database, observe the plan regression, then recover by updating statistics.
Build a skewed dataset to demonstrate parameter sniffing behavior and document two mitigations at the concept level.
Write a one-page incident report for a lab slowdown you induced, including timeline and root cause.
objectives: Follow a repeatable triage order: scope, measure, hypothesize, change one thing, verify.
Use wait statistics and query stats to find bottlenecks instead of guessing.
Recognize missing-index and stale-statistics symptoms in query plans.
Know when a problem belongs to the database and when it belongs to the app, network, or storage.
modules.title: Performance Troubleshooting Basics

checkpoints: The assessment flags a deprecated feature that is actively used. What are your options?
After migration the app connects, but one report returns wrong results. Where do you look first?
Why must logins be migrated separately from the database backup?
Define 'migration success' in measurable terms before the cutover begins.
keyConcepts: Discovery: inventorying everything that moves (data, jobs, logins, linked servers, code)
Compatibility levels and deprecated features
Downtime windows and cutover planning
Migration methods (backup/restore, detach/attach, export/import, replication) and their trade-offs
Login and user mapping: fixing orphaned users after a move
Validation: row counts, checksums, and application smoke tests
Rollback planning: deciding in advance when and how you go back
Post-migration steps: refreshing statistics and re-establishing baselines
labs: Inventory your lab database: list every non-data object (jobs, logins, procedures, linked references) that must migrate with it.
Run the platform's compatibility assessment tooling against the lab database and triage each finding as blocker, warning, or noise.
Perform a backup/restore migration to a fresh container and fix the orphaned users/logins that result.
Run a timed dry-run cutover from a checklist, then hold a retrospective on what slipped.
Write a rollback plan for your migration and mark the point of no return.
objectives: Inventory a source database completely: size, features in use, and dependencies.
Run compatibility checks and classify findings as blockers vs warnings.
Choose a migration method and justify the choice against downtime constraints.
Execute a practice migration to a container and validate row counts and application connectivity.
modules.title: Migration Planning and Execution

checkpoints: Fragmentation measures 5% on a large index. Do you rebuild? Justify with the trade-offs.
Your forecast shows the log volume hitting 80% full in 60 days. What are your options?
A maintenance job overlaps business hours and blocks users. How do you reschedule it safely?
What breaks if statistics updates are skipped for a month?
keyConcepts: The maintenance triad: integrity checks, index maintenance, statistics updates
Fragmentation: what it is, how it is measured, and when it actually matters
Rebuild vs reorganize trade-offs: offline vs online, log impact, duration
Statistics maintenance strategies: automatic vs scheduled manual updates
History cleanup: job history, backup history, and audit retention
Capacity forecasting from trend data with headroom targets
Maintenance windows and minimizing production impact
Runbook documentation that your future on-call self will thank you for
labs: Fragment a lab index with random updates, measure fragmentation, then compare rebuild vs reorganize outcomes.
Build a weekly maintenance script (integrity check, index maintenance, statistics update, history cleanup) and run it end to end.
Collect repeated file-growth samples, chart the trend, and project when each volume reaches 80% full.
Run maintenance during a simulated business-hours load and measure the impact on concurrent user queries.
Write the maintenance runbook: what runs, when, expected duration, and how to back out.
objectives: Build a maintenance plan covering integrity checks, index maintenance, and statistics updates.
Explain fragmentation and when rebuild vs reorganize (or the platform equivalent) applies.
Forecast storage and compute growth from trend data.
Schedule maintenance to minimize impact on production workloads.
modules.title: Capacity Planning and Maintenance

objectives: Install, configure, and operate a relational database server on free editions or containers following vendor-neutral best practices.
Design and execute backup and recovery strategies that meet stated RPO and RTO targets.
Harden a database instance using least privilege, role-based access, auditing, and encryption.
Monitor production-style health signals (waits, locks, space, slow queries) and triage common performance incidents.
Plan and execute a lift-and-shift migration and build a sustainable maintenance and capacity plan.
